context.guidance: Protect each Tier A and Tier B Personal Data Element at field or column level before it is stored, with keys held outside the data store, so that a database dump or a restored backup does not reveal the values. Disk or volume encryption protects only the storage medium, so it lowers severity without clearing the Finding. Until DPDP §44(2) omits IT Act §43A, that section's reasonable-security duty applies alongside Rule 6(1)(a).

value.fix: The security answer is already protected at field level before storage, because the model setter replaces it with security.hmac(answer). The weak spot is the key and the hash type. In the standard version of this code base (OWASP Juice Shop, lib/insecurity.ts), security.hmac uses a fast HMAC-SHA256 with a fixed key written into the source code. I can't see lib/insecurity.ts in the evidence, so check it to confirm. If it holds, anyone with a database dump can read the key from the code and quickly guess the answers, which are short and easy to predict. That means a dump or restored backup can still reveal them. Recommended fix: (1) Remove the fixed key. Load a high-entropy secret (a 'pepper') at runtime from a KMS, HSM or secrets manager, never from the source code or the database, and rotate it with a version ID stored next to each hash. (2) The answer only ever needs to be checked, never read back, so replace the plain HMAC with a slow, salted one-way hash. For example: argon2id(normalize(answer), per-record random salt), then HMAC-SHA256 the result with the pepper, or encrypt it with AES-GCM using a KMS-managed key. Normalize before hashing (trim, lowercase, Unicode NFKC) so correct answers still match. Store the salt and key version, not the plaintext. (3) Check answers with argon2.verify plus a constant-time comparison of the pepper step. Never compare by recomputing a deterministic value in a database WHERE clause. (4) Migration: treat existing hashes as compromised, because the old key is public. Make users re-enroll their security answer, or set a flag that forces a reset, and do not rehash the old values. (5) Add a test checking that the stored column holds no plaintext or old-style HMAC values and that no key appears in the repo or database. Also add a secret-scanning rule for the old key. Disk or volume encryption alone does not close this finding. Tie the control to DPDP Rule 6(1)(a) and to IT Act §43A's reasonable-security duty, which still applies until DPDP §44(2) repeals it.
